author: silver state times
title: CASAT employees and University Police recognized for lifesaving response to cardiac emergency
text:
A contractor working on a flooring project at the Center for the Application of Substance Abuse Technologies (CASAT) offices at the University of Nevada, Reno School of Public Health suffered a sudden cardiac arrest on May 29. Several CASAT employees—Manda Brown, Michelle Berry, Bryana Guerra-Carrera, Sarah DiNatale, Kaitlyn Witt and Sophia Bassi—responded immediately by calling 911, starting CPR and bringing an automated external defibrillator (AED) to the scene. The team continued care until first responders arrived.
University Police Department Northern Command’s Officer Mario Mendieta was first to arrive and took over CPR efforts. Officer Ian Knight then arrived to help direct Reno Fire and REMSA Health personnel. “The CASAT team and the responding University Police Department Northern Command officers’ quick thinking, calm response and willingness to act under pressure truly exemplify the very best of our community,” said Muge Akpinar-Elci, M.D., MPH, dean of the School of Public Health. “This is a testament to what’s possible when a community is prepared and ready to act.”
Josh Reynolds, deputy chief with University Police Department – Northern Command, said: “Officer Mendieta’s prompt response, decisive actions, and continued life-saving efforts helped sustain the victim during a critical medical emergency and contributed to the chain of survival that ultimately resulted in the restoration of the victim’s heartbeat and transport to definitive medical care. This successful outcome was also the result of a coordinated response involving our public safety partners and the CASAT team who stepped forward in a time of need. Their collective actions demonstrate the shared commitment to protecting one another.”
After several defibrillation attempts by Reno Fire and REMSA crews, they were able to restore the contractor’s heartbeat before transporting him for treatment at Saint Mary’s Regional Medical Center; he is now recovering at home. The immediate administration of CPR and AED use before fire crews arrived were likely key factors in his revival.
Michelle Berry said, “I am incredibly proud of how staff responded that day. In an unpredictable and stressful moment, they acted, and because of that, someone is alive today. This is also a powerful reminder of why CPR and AED training matter.” According to both American Heart Association guidance on CPR effectiveness after cardiac arrest as well as American Red Cross information about decreased survival rates with delayed intervention times,
immediate action can significantly improve outcomes.
The CASAT staff members involved were honored during a June 10 Reno City Council meeting alongside police officers Mendieta and Knight as well as members from Reno Fire Department and REMSA Health.
